Subjugate

SUB-juh-gayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To subjugate is to conquer and bring under control by force.

Historical records describe the empire's brutal campaign to subjugate every kingdom along the trade route.

Worked Example

Rather than negotiating a treaty, the conquering general chose to subjugate the coastal cities outright, installing his own officials to replace every local ruler.

The general didn't just win a battle -- he took total, forced control over the people and their government. That complete domination by force is exactly what subjugate means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conquer: To conquer is to defeat a place or people by force, and the story can end with the victory itself -- an army conquers a city in a day. To subjugate stresses what comes after the battle: the defeated people are held down and kept under the winner's control, often for years.

dominate: To dominate is to hold the controlling position -- a team can dominate a league and a firm can dominate a market, with no armies involved. To subjugate is narrower and harsher: it means a people has been brought under control by military force and is kept there against its will.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

liberate: to set free from control or oppression

emancipate: to free from legal, social, or political restrictions

Where it sits · how completely a people is dominated — govern → subjugate → enslave

govern vs. subjugate: To govern a people is simply to administer and rule them, perhaps with their full consent -- far milder than to subjugate them, which means forcing them under control they never chose.

enslave vs. subjugate: To enslave people is to strip them of freedom entirely, an even more total and personal domination than subjugate usually implies.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sub-

prefix — sub-: under (Latin)

root — jug-

root — jug-: a yoke (from Latin jugum, the wooden bar used to harness oxen together)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Subjugate is built from sub- ('under') + jug- ('a yoke,' from Latin jugum, the wooden bar used to harness oxen together) + -ate (a verb ending) -- literally 'to put under the yoke,' the way oxen were harnessed for forced labor. It came to mean conquering and forcing a people under control.

Root Check

Word Choice

Subjugate is a strong, often historical or political word -- it describes forcing an entire people or group under control, not simply winning a small argument. Compare it with usurp, which describes seizing a single position of power, and succumb, which describes the opposite -- giving in to a stronger force rather than exerting one.
